video_title: Bloomberg Businessweek Daily Live From Uncharted Summit | Bloomberg Businessweek Daily 6/26/2026
gist: Broadcast live from the Uncharted Summit in Southampton against a tape where chip stocks are being pummeled and investors pulled money from US equities for the first time in three months: UBS private wealth advisor Allie McCartney argues a post-Fed-guidance 'regime change,' narrative ping-pong and a midterm year keep volatility structural, while a long-delayed wave of private-company liquidity is about to hit markets. Guests from Carta, Domain Money, Poppi and Sentient Jet each read the same AI-wealth cycle from a different angle - startup formation, advice fees, CPG shelf space and private-jet demand.

themes.theme: Post-guidance Fed regime and structural volatility

insights.claim: UBS private wealth advisor Allie McCartney says a regime change at the Fed that ends the era of detailed fed speak, projections and dot-plot dissection will itself increase volatility, because capital allocators lose the certainty they anchor on.
insights.speaker: Allie McCartney
insights.so_what: If forward guidance thins out, expect wider dispersion around data prints and less mean-reverting rate vol; position for higher realized vol rather than trading the dots.
insights.quote: we have a major regime change at the fed. We have a market that is obsessed with fed speak, projections, talk, long statements, dissecting dots. We're not going to get that anymore.

insights.claim: McCartney defines volatility as a constant mismatch between buyers and sellers and says markets are currently in a 'ping pong event in narratives' where Micron's strong earnings lift chips one day and Apple's parts inflation from expensive memory sinks the market the next.
insights.speaker: Allie McCartney
insights.so_what: A narrative-driven tape rewards mean-reversion and vol-selling into single-headline moves rather than trend-following the sector rotation.
insights.quote: Volatility is a constant mismatch between buyers and sellers.

insights.claim: McCartney stacks three volatility drivers - the Fed regime change, the chips-versus-AI-infrastructure-spending narrative fight plus the war in Iran, and a midterm election year following a shocking New York City election result - and expects continued fragility in markets.
insights.speaker: Allie McCartney
insights.so_what: Frames 2026 second-half risk as event-driven and political rather than earnings-driven; hedge around election and geopolitical catalysts.
insights.quote: we just had a quite shocking election result in New York City. We're probably going to get more of those.

insights.claim: Despite the macro noise, McCartney argues the micro is solid - average or median companies delivering roughly 5 to 8% earnings growth alongside a secular AI evolution - so the macro has been heavily discounted apart from the last couple of days.
insights.speaker: Allie McCartney
insights.so_what: Supports buying macro-driven drawdowns in earnings-compounding names rather than de-risking wholesale.

themes.theme: The delayed private-liquidity wave hitting markets

insights.claim: McCartney says exits that were underwritten to happen in three to five years are now taking seven to eleven years, leaving Silicon Valley flush with innovation but not with capital.
insights.speaker: Allie McCartney
insights.so_what: Quantifies the DPI drought behind LP frustration; a re-opening of exit windows is the single biggest swing factor for venture fund cash flows.
insights.quote: things we thought were going to be liquid and have events, either IPO's or purchases three, 4 or 5 years in, we're now seven, ten, 11 years in.

insights.claim: McCartney predicts a sea change in the amount of liquidity about to enter markets from private companies and venture funds, with both positive and negative consequences for public and private markets, arriving at a moment of geopolitical uncertainty and market highs.
insights.speaker: Allie McCartney
insights.so_what: A liquidity wave into a market at highs means both a bid for diversifying assets and supply pressure from lockup expiries - watch lockup calendars on recent listings.
insights.quote: I think we are about to get a sea change in terms of the amount of liquidity that can go into the market and that venture funds can charge on.

insights.claim: About half of McCartney's clients are private-company founders whom she works with before liquidity, structuring concentrated loans and derivatives so they can buy assets against illiquid stakes and take chips off the table ahead of lockup expiry.
insights.speaker: Allie McCartney
insights.so_what: Pre-liquidity lending and hedging against private shares is a growth business for wealth platforms and a source of latent selling pressure once lockups lift.
insights.quote: I'm calling this the space summer. The way, um, the way restaurants are behaving, the way real estate and the Hamptons are behaving. You can just see that people feel flush.

insights.claim: McCartney says clients coming out of concentrated positions are doing a large amount of buying to diversify, pointing to the Russell up 20% and Europe outperforming the US as places that are working.
insights.speaker: Allie McCartney
insights.so_what: Diversification flows out of concentrated tech wealth favor small caps and non-US equities over more mega-cap tech.
insights.quote: We have Europe outperforming the U.S., so there are lots of things that are working.

themes.theme: Chip selloff, tech outflows and the AI payoff question

insights.claim: Investors pulled money from American stocks for the first time in three months with record withdrawals from tech funds, as chipmakers were hit by another burst of selling.
insights.speaker: Amy Morris
insights.so_what: Record tech-fund outflows alongside a flat index are a positioning signal - the de-risking is concentrated in semis, not the broad market.
insights.quote: Chipmakers got pummeled by another burst of selling investors pulling money from American stocks for the first time in three months. Record withdrawals from tech funds.

insights.claim: The semiconductor complex broke down hard on the session with all 30 members of the chip index lower, the index down about 4.5%, ON Semiconductor down 24% and Micron down more than 4%, even as roughly 324 S&P 500 members traded higher.
insights.speaker: Carol Massar
insights.so_what: A single-sector unwind against broad market breadth argues the selloff is chip-specific, not systemic - a pair-trade setup rather than an index short.
insights.quote: All 30 members of the stocks are lower. Uh, we got, uh, wow. We got some companies making big moves. Even the best performer, Nvidia, is down half a percentage point.

insights.claim: A report that OpenAI could postpone plans to go public weighed on sentiment alongside chip price increases feeding into products like Apple and Microsoft, triggering fears about the staying power of chip demand.
insights.speaker: Amy Morris
insights.so_what: An OpenAI IPO delay removes the marquee liquidity event the AI complex was priced against; watch it as a sentiment marker for the whole private AI cohort.
insights.quote: a report that OpenAI could postpone plans to go public also weighed on sentiment

insights.claim: SpaceX's blockbuster bond sale is widening sharply in the secondary market with paper losses of about $305 million, which traders read as evidence fast-money accounts piled in to flip the deal for a quick profit.
insights.speaker: Amy Morris
insights.so_what: A marquee private-AI-adjacent credit deal breaking syndicate is an early warning on demand for the next wave of private-company debt issuance.
insights.quote: SpaceX's blockbuster bond sale is weakening quickly in the secondary market, with traders saying they cannot recall another recent deal that widened this sharply. Paper losses totaling about $305 million.

themes.theme: Carta's cap-table view of startup formation

insights.claim: Carta CRO Jeff Perry says AI-driven wealth and recent IPOs will foster a new cohort of founders who fund themselves initially but then seek outside investment, which is why Carta expanded from cap tables into fund administration.
insights.speaker: Jeff Perry
insights.so_what: Company-formation volume, not just megacap capex, is a downstream beneficiary of AI liquidity events - bullish for the venture services stack.
insights.quote: what we'll start to see more of is more companies being created because of the wealth being generated out of some of these AI companies

insights.claim: Carta now has over 50,000 companies on its cap table platform and works with about 2,500 venture and private equity firms, giving it direct visibility into private-company formation and valuation.
insights.speaker: Jeff Perry
insights.so_what: Scale metrics make Carta's proprietary dataset a leading indicator on private-market activity that public investors cannot otherwise see.
insights.quote: We now have 50,000 plus companies on the the cap table platform

insights.claim: Carta runs a free 'launch' tier for companies that have raised under $1 million or have 25 or fewer stakeholders, explicitly as a land-and-expand funnel that converts successful founders to paid plans.
insights.speaker: Jeff Perry
insights.so_what: Classic freemium capture of the founder cohort - the conversion rate on that funnel is the key variable for Carta's long-term revenue.
insights.quote: companies that are early stage raised less than $1 million or have 25 stakeholders or less on our on their cap table. We offer a free platform for them.

insights.claim: Carta has completed five acquisitions in the last nine months, most notably a CRM bolted onto its fund-admin ERP platform and a law firm, so that compliance and risk work currently paid to outside law firms can be delivered through Carta's AI tool.
insights.speaker: Jeff Perry
insights.so_what: A software company buying a law firm to disintermediate legal fees with AI is a template for services-margin capture worth watching across professional services.
insights.quote: We've done five acquisitions over the course of the last nine months.

themes.theme: Attacking the 1% AUM fee for the emerging affluent

insights.claim: Adam Dell says Domain Money is built to blow apart the 1% AUM fee, arguing that over a lifetime that fee is the equivalent of giving your advisor a house, and replaces it with a flat fee and a dedicated certified financial planner.
insights.speaker: Adam Dell
insights.so_what: Direct fee pressure on the traditional wealth management revenue model - watch flat-fee competitors as a margin risk to RIAs and wirehouses.
insights.quote: We are trying to blow apart the 1% AUM fee that most people pay to their financial advisor, which, if you do the math over the course of a lifetime, is essentially the equivalent of giving your advisor a house.

insights.claim: Dell says robo-advisors failed to kill human advice because they only solve taxable investment accounts and ignore 529 plans, 401(k)s, and cash-flow and budgeting decisions, and because clients want a bespoke human they trust when complexity and the cost of being wrong are high.
insights.speaker: Adam Dell
insights.so_what: Explains why bank wealth-management revenue keeps compounding despite cheap automation; the disruptable part is the fee structure, not the human.
insights.quote: If you want a digital AI advisor today, you can get it from ChatGPT for free, essentially. But people don't want that.

insights.claim: Domain Money's average client is 42 years old with household income of $364,000 and net worth of $1.3 million - a segment Dell says sits just below the traditional wealth management threshold and gets assigned junior advisors.
insights.speaker: Adam Dell
insights.so_what: Defines the underserved 'emerging affluent' wedge precisely enough to size it as a competitive threat or acquisition target.
insights.quote: our average customers. 42 years old. Household income of 364. Net worth of 1.3 million to the right smack below the traditional wealth management sector.

insights.claim: Dell puts the addressable market at 29 million Americans in that demographic and argues Domain Money can serve them profitably because technology plus a scripted service-delivery model stops clients from driving the relationship into unproductive market chat.
insights.speaker: Adam Dell
insights.so_what: Unit economics, not demand, were the historic barrier to serving this segment - if the model holds it invites wirehouse and RIA-consolidator acquisition interest.
insights.quote: there is 29 million people in the United States who fall within the demographic that I described earlier

insights.claim: Dell says his clients are not asking for private credit or alternatives at all - they want correct tax allocation, allocation across their 401(k), and consistent goal-based planning.
insights.speaker: Adam Dell
insights.so_what: A direct counterpoint to the industry push to democratize alts into mass-affluent channels - retail demand there may be thinner than sponsors assume.
insights.quote: Our client is not looking for private credit or access to alternatives. It's really about the correct tax allocation and strategy and minimizing those taxes.

insights.claim: Dell frames the long-term prize as clients who will have $5 million in 20 years and will inherit $84 trillion over that period, which is why Domain Money intends to keep expanding services as client complexity increases.
insights.speaker: Adam Dell
insights.so_what: The great wealth transfer is the underwriting assumption for mass-affluent advice platforms; capturing clients pre-inheritance is the land grab.
insights.quote: this client will have $5 million in 20 years, and they'll inherit 84 trillion over the course of the next 20.

themes.theme: Falling token costs as operating leverage

insights.claim: Dell says Domain Money consumes a lot of tokens ingesting, parsing and extracting data from documents, and that the cost of tokens is declining so precipitously that the company's own costs are declining.
insights.speaker: Adam Dell
insights.so_what: A live example of AI deflation flowing straight into gross margin for document-heavy financial services - a margin tailwind not yet in most models.
insights.quote: the cost of tokens is declining so precipitously that really our costs are declining

insights.claim: Dell argues the real AI opportunity is business-process disruption at the operational level, and that any small or large business owner not actively finding ways to use AI to improve cost and efficiency is doing the wrong thing.
insights.speaker: Adam Dell
insights.so_what: Points ROI toward opex reduction across the long tail of businesses rather than headline model capex - relevant to software adoption forecasts.

themes.theme: Functional beverage playbook after a $2B exit

insights.claim: Poppi co-founder Allison Ellsworth, who sold the brand to PepsiCo for $1.95 billion last year, says beverages are brutally capital intensive - shipping liquid across the US, manufacturing, shelf life - and that success came from hiring industry insiders after a Shark Tank deal opened her network.
insights.speaker: Allison Ellsworth
insights.so_what: Sets the realistic bar for beverage startup underwriting - distribution relationships and working capital, not product, are the binding constraints.
insights.quote: It's capital intensive. You have to have a lot of money. You're shipping liquid across the U.S., manufacturing shelf life.

insights.claim: Ellsworth's product rule is that a better-for-you beverage must be only 10% to 30% better, not 100% better, because taste is king and America still wants full flavor - a lesson she says explains Poppi's win over more austere health products.
insights.speaker: Allison Ellsworth
insights.so_what: A screening heuristic for CPG bets: reject products that sacrifice taste for health claims, including carbonated protein concepts.
insights.quote: I think it has to be just 10% better or 30% better. It can't be 100% better for you. People still want full flavor.

insights.claim: Ellsworth says clean-label products cost meaningfully more because artificial ingredients are cheap, but that the single largest cost is packaging, followed by shipping - not the ingredients themselves.
insights.speaker: Allison Ellsworth
insights.so_what: Reframes better-for-you CPG margin analysis around packaging and freight inputs rather than ingredient inflation.
insights.quote: really what the most expensive thing is the packaging

insights.claim: For her new fall-launching beverage Ellsworth is self-funding roughly $2.5 million and will only accept strategic money that brings distributor relationships, retailers, celebrities or influencer talent, deliberately starting in better-for-you retailers like Whole Foods, Target and Sprouts before going mass.
insights.speaker: Allison Ellsworth
insights.so_what: Post-exit founders can dictate terms and bypass generic capital - a signal that strategic and distribution-linked money outcompetes pure financial capital in CPG.
insights.quote: we are only going to take strategic money that can actually make a move

themes.theme: Private aviation as an AI-wealth proxy

insights.claim: Sentient Jet CRO Alan Hawley says the private jet card market grew about 11% year over year in the US and 4% globally, with Sentient adding 300 new customers in nine months to surpass 7,000 total.
insights.speaker: Alan Hawley
insights.so_what: Hard growth numbers on discretionary ultra-premium spending - a real-time read on whether paper AI wealth is converting into consumption.
insights.quote: the market as a whole has actually increased, uh, I think 11% year over year. Um, here in the U.S., I think for 4% globally, we've we've seen 300 new customers in the last nine, nine months. So we're over 7000 customers now.

insights.claim: Hawley says the flyer base is skewing younger into the mid-forties, driven by technology wealth, and that Sentient now accepts payment in crypto because its customer base demanded it.
insights.speaker: Alan Hawley
insights.so_what: Crypto acceptance at a luxury-services incumbent is a concrete adoption datapoint, and a younger flyer cohort extends the demand runway for jet cards.
insights.quote: we now take payments in crypto. That was a demand from our customer base

insights.claim: Hawley says higher jet fuel prices from the overseas conflict have not slowed the business at all because buyers are purchasing time, so the decision criterion has shifted from cost to reliability and consistency of service.
insights.speaker: Alan Hawley
insights.so_what: Demand for private aviation looks price-inelastic to fuel, which protects margins at asset-light brokers during energy spikes.
insights.quote: What we're finding is that people still need to fly, and in fact, the onus has moved from maybe looking at cost to reliability and consistency.

insights.claim: Sentient runs an asset-light model, unlike sister company Flexjet, curating a certified operator network into which roughly 30% of total operators qualify, with every flight monitored in real time and 24/7 support.
insights.speaker: Alan Hawley
insights.so_what: Asset-light brokerage avoids fleet capex and residual-value risk - a structurally different risk profile from fractional-ownership operators.
insights.quote: around 30% of total operators make it into one network

insights.claim: Hawley reports over 100 bookings in the last month tied to the World Cup alone, with demand driven by last-minute flexibility because customers do not know where their team will play.
insights.speaker: Alan Hawley
insights.so_what: Quantifies a discrete event-driven revenue bump for private aviation and hospitality around the 2026 World Cup.
insights.quote: We've had over 100 bookings in the last month for the World Cup alone
